►  BREAKING: MAJOR ENGAGEMENT UNDERWAY NEAR BRUSSELS — WELLINGTON AND BLÜCHER FACE NAPOLEON AT WATERLOO  ►  DISPATCHES EXPECTED THIS EVENING  ►  FUNDS FALL SHARPLY ON THE EXCHANGE
Europe | Sunday 18 June 1815 | Last updated: 11:42 GMT
Europe — Top Stories

Napoleon meets Wellington on fields of Waterloo — the fate of Europe in the balance

The Imperial French Army, led by Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte, has engaged the Duke of Wellington's Allied forces and Field Marshal Blücher's Prussian army at a small Belgian village south of Brussels. Observers say the battle is the most consequential since Leipzig.

By our Continental Correspondent, William Hazlitt-Forster  |  Near Quatre Bras, Belgium  |  18 June 1815, 09:15 GMT

Artist's impression of the morning engagement south of Brussels. The battle is expected to decide the future of the Napoleonic Wars. (BBC Illustration)

Dawn broke this Sunday morning over the sodden fields of Belgium to reveal two of the great armies of Europe arrayed for what both sides believe will be a decisive engagement. The Emperor Napoleon, who returned to power barely one hundred days ago following his escape from the island of Elba, has marched his reconstituted Grande Armée northward with characteristic speed, aiming to defeat the Allied and Prussian forces before they can combine their full strength.

Arthur Wellesley, the Duke of Wellington, commanding a multinational Allied force numbering some 68,000 men, has positioned his troops along the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean, near the hamlet of Waterloo in the Duchy of Brabant. Field Marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher's Prussian army, though badly mauled at Ligny two days prior, is reported to be marching to the Duke's assistance.

"I have the greatest confidence that we shall succeed, though the affair will be a damned near-run thing, I can tell you."
— Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington, reported by aide-de-camp this morning

Fighting is understood to have begun in earnest around half past eleven in the morning, with a French assault upon the fortified farm of Hougoumont on the Allied right flank. The sound of heavy cannon fire has been reported by residents of Brussels, some twelve miles to the north, where considerable anxiety prevails. Many citizens have fled northward along the Brussels–Antwerp road.

Our correspondent reports that morale among Wellington's troops, which includes British, Dutch, Belgian and German contingents, appears resolute, though the previous day's hard marching in torrential rain has left many men fatigued. Napoleon is expected to deploy his celebrated Imperial Guard should the initial assaults prove insufficient to break the Allied line.
